body.objective: Students will be able to count syncopated rhythms.
successCriteria: I can count syncopated rhythms with subdivision
I can perform rhythms with ties and off-beat accents accurately
I can use a sight-reading routine before playing
body.hook: Syncopation is what makes music groove: the accent lands where you don't expect it, between the beats. Funk, Latin, jazz and almost every pop song depend on it, and band music is full of it too.

vocabulary.definition: Stressing a weak beat or the off-beat instead of the strong beat.
Dividing the beat into smaller parts, such as "1 & 2 &."
A curved line joining two notes of the same pitch so they are held as one.
Playing music you have not seen before.
The order of repeats, endings and jumps in a piece.

study.title: Between the Beats
study.question: How do musicians read and feel syncopated rhythms?
study.passage:
Part 1, Subdivide (10 minutes): With a metronome at 80, count "1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &" aloud while tapping the beat with your foot. Clap only the "&s."
Part 2, Pattern ladder (15 minutes): Clap and count each pattern in 4/4, then play it on one note:
(a) quarter, quarter, quarter, quarter (no syncopation)
(b) eighth, quarter, eighth, quarter, quarter (the "1 &(2)" figure: accent on "&" of 1, held through 2)
(c) eighth, quarter, quarter, quarter, eighth (accents fall on "&s")
(d) quarter tied to an eighth across beat 3 (the tie hides beat 3)
Rule: Write the counts under each note before you play. Ties: count the second note but don't play it.
Part 3, Sight-reading routine "STARS" (10 minutes): S: sharps and flats (key signature), T: time signature and tempo, A: accidentals, R: rhythms (circle the tricky ones and count them), S: signs (dynamics, articulations, repeats, road map). Spend 60 seconds on STARS, then play without stopping.
Part 4, Band read (15 minutes): Sight-read a short exercise as a band using STARS. Keep going even if you make a mistake.
study.source: Original rhythm workshop written for this lesson; the STARS routine is a common music education strategy.

practice.q: What should you do if you make a mistake when sight-reading?
practice.a: Keep going and find the next beat.

practice.q: What is a road map in music?
practice.a: The order of repeats, endings and jumps.

practice.q: Why tap your foot on the beat?
practice.a: To keep the pulse steady while rhythms move around it.

practice.q: Why do syncopated notes often feel early?
practice.a: They start on the off-beat before the main beat.

practice.q: How does a tie across the middle of a bar create syncopation?
practice.a: It hides a strong beat so the accent falls elsewhere.

practice.q: Why should you never stop when sight-reading in a band?
practice.a: The band keeps going; stopping makes you lose your place.

practice.q: How would you practise a tricky syncopated bar?
practice.a: Count aloud, clap, play slowly with a metronome, then speed up.
